meta.title: Discrete-time control: ZOH models, deadbeat response and controller emulation
meta.tools: Exact zero-order-hold discretisation (matrix exponential) checked against scipy.signal.cont2discrete, pole mapping z = e^{sT}, deadbeat state feedback by discrete Ackermann, inter-sample simulation of the continuous plant, forward-Euler / backward-Euler / Tustin emulation of a continuous compensator
meta.summary: Model a continuous plant as seen by a computer, design a deadbeat controller that settles in exactly n samples (something no continuous linear controller can do), look between the samples, and show how the choice of discretisation rule decides whether an emulated analog controller stays stable.
meta.problem: A digital controller only sees samples and only changes its output at sample instants. What is the plant from its point of view, and what can it do that an analog one cannot?
meta.theory:
With a zero-order hold, $x_{k+1}=e^{AT}x_k+\int_0^Te^{Aτ}dτ\,B\,u_k$ exactly; poles map as $z=e^{sT}$. State feedback placing all n poles at z = 0 makes $(A_d-B_dK)^n=0$: any initial state is driven to zero in n steps (deadbeat). The required
effort grows roughly as $1/T^2$ for a double-integrator-like plant. Emulating a compensator pole s = −a: forward Euler $z=1-aT$ (unstable for $aT>2$), backward Euler $z=1/(1+aT)$ and Tustin $z=\frac{1-aT/2}{1+aT/2}$ (always stable).
meta.method:
Plant $G= rac{1}{s(s+1)}$ (motor with inertia), T = 0.2 s. Deadbeat gain by Ackermann on (A_d, B_d); plant simulated continuously between samples (100 sub-steps). Effort scaling for T = 0.2, 0.1, 0.05. Emulation: lead compensator
$C= rac{10(s+1)}{s+20}$ at T = 0.02…0.2 s with the three rules; stability of the discrete compensator and of the closed loop.

rows.quantity: Own ZOH discretisation vs scipy.signal.cont2discrete (max difference)
Discrete poles = e^{sT}: second pole e^{−T}
ZOH adds a sampling zero: zero of the pulse transfer function (≈ −1 for small T; exact value from the formula)
Deadbeat step: position error after exactly 2 samples
… and no inter-sample ripple afterwards (max |y − 1| for t > 2T)
Deadbeat effort: peak |u| ratio when T is halved (≈ 4× for a double-integrator-like plant)
Forward Euler: compensator pole leaves the unit circle at T = 2/a
Backward Euler and Tustin: compensator stable at every tested T (1 = yes)
